title: I interviewed the Jubilee CEO on platforming bigotry
content:
I interviewed the CEO of Jubilee about his company and his editorial process. You can watch the full interview on my YouTube page.

Jubilee is a YouTube behemoth with over 10.2 subscribers. It employs dozens of people in a sprawling office in Los Angeles. The channel puts out a variety of shows, but it is most famous for its debate style content. Recent videos include “Anorexic vs Obese” or “Flat Earthers vs Scientists: Can We Trust Science?” Jubilee’s video “1 Republican vs. 25 Kamala Harris Voters (Feat. Ben Shapiro)” was the fifth most-watched piece of election content on YouTube last year.

The company was founded by Jason Y. Lee, a former Obama staffer who claims that he wants to build the “Disney of empathy,” a media company that will help people connect and come together over our shared humanity. The company is planning to launch a dating app, expand off YouTube into card games and other products, and hopes to host the 2028 U.S. presidential debate.

But what Jubilee really does is monetize division by producing an endless stream of ragebait and “XYZ gets owned” shortform video clips. Every few months, these clips go viral and those lucky few who haven’t yet learned about Jubilee are forced to confront it.

This is exactly what happened this week after Jubilee published their latest video, “ 1 Progressive vs 20 Far-Right Conservatives” featuring Mehdi Hasan. Hasan, undeniably one of the best debaters online, fruitlessly attempts to debate a crowd of people who openly admit to being fascist. “Jubilee Media's done it again: taking 20 people with extremist views and putting them into a 90 minute video knowing that they'll say extreme things and get an extreme amount of attention,” reporter Julia Alexander posted.

Matt Bernstein did an excellent takedown of Jubilee’s rage bait business model earlier this year, but I think that the company’s videos are especially corrosive at a time when far right extremism is pervasive and Trump is in power. “Jubilee’s entire operation revolves around generating adsense $$$ from clicks on outrage content designed to be as extreme, hateful, and violent as possible,” Bernstein noted. “If YouTube demonetizes the channel, the operation would collapse.”

It feels especially bleak that Jubilee’s latest video was published the same week as the Nelk Boys sponcon-style interview with Benjamin Netanyahu. The Nelk Boys, pro-Trump YouTubers who built their platform on getting drunk and performing increasingly outrageous stunts, are now a major voice in political media. Following their conversation with Netanyahu they invited Nick Fuentes and Sneako, two avowed anti-semites, onto their stream to “present the other side.” Jewish comedian Adam Friedland and Hasan Piker also appeared to share their reactions. In the end, the Nelk Boys didn’t seem very moved.

I’m not against the shift towards more independent media, or “influencer” driven media as a whole. There is tons of independent media (hopefully this newsletter included!) that exists to challenge power. Traditional media also regularly platforms evil people and the corporate mainstream media primarily exists to reinforce elite power structures.

But I do think that we’re in a bleak place where people still haven’t grasped the nature of the attention economy, and, as a creator, trying to build a sustainable business model when you’re competing with an endless tsunami of fascist slop and branded content is incredibly difficult. (So thank you for being a paid subscriber!). I think the media environment will likely continue to get worse before it gets better.
